notes.front: In the Nexus Guide, what is product structure?
notes.back: The degree to which different concerns are independently separated in the product.
notes.explanation: The Guide names it as one of two mismatches that often cause dependencies: it greatly affects the complexity of creating an integrated product release.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Product structure: The degree to which different concerns are independently separated in the product will greatly affect the complexity of creating an integrated product release.
notes.example: Like the rooms of a house, each with its own door, but in a product: the invoicing code kept apart from the search code, so either can change on its own.

notes.front: In the Nexus Guide, what is communication structure?
notes.back: The way people communicate within and between teams, which affects their ability to get work done.
notes.explanation: It is the second mismatch the Guide names as a common cause of dependencies; delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Communication structure: The way that people communicate within and between teams affects their ability to get work done; delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.
notes.example: Like the wiring between offices in a building, but for people: who can phone whom directly, and whose questions wait for a meeting.

notes.front: What is Nexus Sprint Planning for?
notes.back: Coordinating the activities of all Scrum Teams within a Nexus for a single Sprint.
notes.explanation: Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team meet with the Product Owner to plan the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The purpose of Nexus Sprint Planning is to coordinate the activities of all Scrum Teams within a Nexus for a single Sprint. Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team and the Product Owner meet to plan the Sprint.
notes.example: Like Sprint Planning for one Scrum Team, but one level up: people from each of five teams and the one Product Owner agree how the Sprint fits together.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Sprint Goal?
notes.back: A single objective for the Nexus: the sum of all the work and Sprint Goals of its Scrum Teams.
notes.explanation: It creates coherence and focus for the Sprint by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Goal is a single objective for the Nexus. It is the sum of all the work and Sprint Goals of the Scrum Teams within the Nexus. It creates coherence and focus for the Nexus for the Sprint by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Goal, but for the whole Nexus: “A traveller can book and pay for a trip on the new app”, which each team’s own goal helps to reach.

notes.front: What is a Nexus Sprint Backlog?
notes.back: The composite of the Nexus Sprint Goal and the Product Backlog items from the individual Scrum Teams’ Sprint Backlogs.
notes.explanation: It is used to highlight dependencies and the flow of work during the Sprint, and is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: A Nexus Sprint Backlog is the composite of the Nexus Sprint Goal and Product Backlog items from the Sprint Backlogs of the individual Scrum Teams. It is used to highlight dependencies and the flow of work during the Sprint. The Nexus Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Backlog, but assembled across the Nexus: every team’s selected items in one view, with the links between teams drawn in.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Daily Scrum for?
notes.back: Identifying integration issues and inspecting progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: Appropriate representatives from the Scrum Teams attend and inspect the current state of the integrated Increment.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Nexus Daily Scrum is to identify any integration issues and inspect progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal. Appropriate representatives from the Scrum Teams attend the Nexus Daily Scrum, inspect the current state of the integrated Increment, and identify integration issues and newly discovered cross-team dependencies or impacts.
notes.example: Like a Daily Scrum, but across teams: one Developer from each team checks whether the work merged overnight still runs together.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Sprint Review?
notes.back: An event at the end of the Sprint to get feedback on the done Integrated Increment and determine future adaptations.
notes.explanation: Because the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for stakeholder feedback, it replaces the individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Review is held at the end of the Sprint to provide feedback on the done Integrated Increment that the Nexus has built over the Sprint and determine future adaptations. Since the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, a Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Review, but for the combined product: stakeholders try the one working app that four teams built together.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Sprint Retrospective for?
notes.back: Planning ways to increase quality and effectiveness across the whole Nexus.
notes.explanation: The Nexus inspects how the last Sprint went, including individuals, teams, interactions, processes, tools and its Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Nexus Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness across the whole Nexus. The Nexus inspects how the last Sprint went with regards to individuals, teams, interactions, processes, tools, and its Definition of Done.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Retrospective, but for the whole Nexus: a look at why three teams kept breaking each other’s builds.

notes.front: According to the Nexus Guide, how far does Nexus extend Scrum?
notes.back: Only where absolutely necessary to minimise and manage dependencies between multiple Scrum Teams.
notes.explanation: It does so while promoting empiricism and the Scrum Values; the Guide calls Nexus a framework for developing and sustaining scaled product delivery.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Nexus is a framework for developing and sustaining scaled product delivery initiatives. It builds upon Scrum, extending it only where absolutely necessary to minimize and manage dependencies between multiple Scrum Teams while promoting empiricism and the Scrum Values.

notes.front: The Nexus Guide says scaled Scrum is still Scrum. What three things does Nexus not do to Scrum?
notes.back: Change its core design or ideas, leave out its elements, or negate its rules.
notes.explanation: The Guide warns that doing so covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Scaled Scrum is still Scrum. Nexus does not change the core design or ideas of Scrum, or leave out elements, or negate the rules of Scrum. Doing so covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless.

notes.front: What is the goal of Nexus, and how does it pursue it?
notes.back: To scale the value a group of Scrum Teams on a single product can deliver, by reducing the complexity they encounter.
notes.explanation: The teams meet that complexity as they collaborate to deliver an integrated, valuable, useful product Increment at least once every Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The goal of Nexus is to scale the value that a group of Scrum Teams, working on a single product, is able to deliver. It does this by reducing the complexity that those teams encounter as they collaborate to deliver an integrated, valuable, useful product Increment at least once every Sprint.

notes.front: To reduce or remove dependencies between teams, what three things does Nexus give opportunities to change?
notes.back: The process, the product structure and the communication structure.
notes.explanation: Two of the three are the structures whose mismatches the Guide names as common causes of dependencies.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Nexus provides opportunities to change the process, product structure, and communication structure to reduce or remove these dependencies.

notes.front: What does the Nexus Guide call reducing the number of people who work on something, and what can it help deliver?
notes.back: Scaling-down; it can be an important practice in delivering more value.
notes.explanation: Adding people and growing the product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration and the communication pathways in decisions.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions. Scaling-down, reducing the number of people who work on something, can be an important practice in delivering more value.

notes.front: According to the Nexus Guide, what are two things that increase when more people work on a larger product?
notes.back: Two of: complexity and dependencies; the need for collaboration; the number of communication pathways in decisions.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it often counterintuitive that scaling the value delivered does not always require adding more people.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: While often counterintuitive, scaling the value that is delivered does not always require adding more people. Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions.

notes.front: Scrum defines three accountabilities within a Scrum Team. Which additional accountability does Nexus introduce?
notes.back: The Nexus Integration Team.
notes.explanation: The three Scrum accountabilities, Developers, Product Owner and Scrum Master, stay as the Scrum Guide prescribes them.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Accountabilities in Nexus”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Scrum framework defines three specific sets of accountabilities within a Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master. These accountabilities are prescribed in the Scrum Guide. In Nexus, an additional accountability is introduced, the Nexus Integration Team.

notes.front: How do Nexus events relate to the regular Scrum events?
notes.back: They are appended to, placed around, or replace regular Scrum events, to augment them.
notes.explanation: As modified, they serve both the overall effort of all Scrum Teams in the Nexus and each individual team.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “The Nexus Framework”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Events are appended to, placed around, or replace regular Scrum events to augment them. As modified, they serve both the overall effort of all Scrum Teams in the Nexus, and each individual team.

notes.front: Among the artifacts Nexus adds to Scrum, what does the Nexus Sprint Backlog exist to do?
notes.back: To assist with transparency during the Sprint.
notes.explanation: It sits beside the same, single Product Backlog that all the Scrum Teams use.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “The Nexus Framework”, p. 5
notes.evidence: All Scrum Teams use the same, single Product Backlog. As the Product Backlog items are refined and made ready, indicators of which team will most likely do the work inside a Sprint are made transparent. A Nexus Sprint Backlog exists to assist with transparency during the Sprint.

notes.front: As Product Backlog items are refined and made ready in a Nexus, what is made transparent?
notes.back: Indicators of which team will most likely do the work inside a Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists this under Nexus artifacts, next to the single Product Backlog that all Scrum Teams use.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “The Nexus Framework”, p. 5
notes.evidence: All Scrum Teams use the same, single Product Backlog. As the Product Backlog items are refined and made ready, indicators of which team will most likely do the work inside a Sprint are made transparent.

notes.front: Besides ensuring a done Integrated Increment each Sprint, what does the Nexus Integration Team’s focus make possible?
notes.back: The accountability of multiple Scrum Teams to come together to create valuable, useful Increments, as Scrum prescribes.
notes.explanation: It connects Scrum’s own expectation of valuable, useful Increments to the combined work of several teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: makes possible the accountability of multiple Scrum Teams to come together to create valuable, useful Increments, as prescribed in Scrum.

notes.front: In a Nexus, who addresses integration issues, and what does the Nexus Integration Team provide?
notes.back: The Scrum Teams address integration issues; the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the Nexus Integration Team should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While Scrum Teams address integration issues within the Nexus, the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration for the Nexus. Integration includes addressing technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a Nexus’ ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment. It should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.

notes.front: In a Nexus, does integration cover only technical issues?
notes.back: No. It includes technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a constantly Integrated Increment.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Integration Team is the focal point for integration, including these constraints.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While Scrum Teams address integration issues within the Nexus, the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration for the Nexus. Integration includes addressing technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a Nexus’ ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment. It should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.

notes.front: Who counts as an “appropriate member” of the Nexus Integration Team, and is its make-up fixed?
notes.back: People with the skills and knowledge to help resolve the Nexus’s current issues; its composition may change over time.
notes.explanation: Membership follows the issues the Nexus faces at any point in time, to reflect its current needs.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Appropriate members are the people with the necessary skills and knowledge to help resolve the issues the Nexus faces at any point in time. Composition of the Nexus Integration Team may change over time to reflect the current needs of a Nexus.

notes.front: What are two common activities the Nexus Integration Team might perform?
notes.back: Two of: coaching, consulting, and highlighting awareness of dependencies and cross-team issues.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the common activities “include” these, so the list is not closed.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Common activities the Nexus Integration Team might perform include coaching, consulting, and highlighting awareness of dependencies and cross-team issues.

notes.front: What does the Nexus Integration Team coach and guide the Scrum Teams to acquire, implement and learn?
notes.back: Practices and tools that improve their ability to produce a valuable, useful Increment.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes this a responsibility of the Nexus Integration Team as a whole.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for coaching and guiding the Scrum Teams to acquire, implement, and learn practices and tools that improve their ability to produce a valuable, useful Increment.

notes.front: In a Nexus, what is the Product Owner accountable for maximising?
notes.back: The value of the product and of the work performed and integrated by the Scrum Teams in the Nexus.
notes.explanation: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, whose single Product Owner has the final say on its contents.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, and as described in Scrum, a Product Backlog has a single Product Owner who has the final say on its contents. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product and the work performed and integrated by the Scrum Teams in a Nexus.

notes.front: Does the Nexus Guide prescribe how the Product Owner carries out effective Product Backlog management?
notes.back: No. How it is done may vary widely across organisations, Nexuses, Scrum Teams and individuals.
notes.explanation: The accountability itself stays with the Product Owner; only the way it is met varies.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management. How this is done may vary widely across organizations, Nexuses, Scrum Teams, and individuals.

notes.front: What is the Scrum Master in the Nexus Integration Team accountable for, and may they also serve a Scrum Team?
notes.back: Ensuring Nexus is understood and enacted as the Nexus Guide describes; yes, they may also be Scrum Master of one or more Scrum Teams.
notes.explanation: The Guide names a Scrum Master as one of the Nexus Integration Team's members, and says this person may also be Scrum Master of one or more Scrum Teams in the Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master in the Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as described in the Nexus Guide. This Scrum Master may also be a Scrum Master in one or more of the Scrum Teams in the Nexus.

notes.front: Which takes precedence: membership in the Nexus Integration Team or in an individual Scrum Team?
notes.back: Nexus Integration Team membership; members work in their Scrum Teams as long as that responsibility is satisfied.
notes.explanation: The Guide says this preference helps ensure that work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Membership in the Nexus Integration Team takes precedence over individual Scrum Team membership. As long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as team members of their respective Scrum Teams. This preference helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.

notes.front: What guides the duration of Nexus events?
notes.back: The length of the corresponding events in the Scrum Guide; Nexus events are timeboxed in addition to them.
notes.explanation: The Guide frames Nexus events as additions to, or extensions of, the events Scrum defines.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Events”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Nexus adds to or extends the events defined by Scrum. The duration of Nexus events is guided by the length of the corresponding events in the Scrum Guide. They are timeboxed in addition to their corresponding Scrum events.

notes.front: Except where the Guide says otherwise, who attends Nexus events?
notes.back: Whichever members of the Nexus are needed to achieve the event’s intended outcome most effectively.
notes.explanation: At scale, it may not be practical for all members of the Nexus to take part to share information or reach agreement.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Events”, p. 7
notes.evidence: At scale, it may not be practical for all members of the Nexus to participate to share information or to come to an agreement. Except where noted, Nexus events are attended by whichever members of the Nexus are needed to achieve the intended outcome of the event most effectively.

notes.front: Does Cross-Team Refinement replace each Scrum Team’s own refinement?
notes.back: No. Where needed, each team continues its own refinement so items are ready for selection in Nexus Sprint Planning.
notes.explanation: Cross-Team Refinement is ongoing, and its frequency, duration and attendance vary to optimise its two purposes.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Cross-Team Refinement”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Cross-Team Refinement is ongoing. The frequency, duration, and attendance of Cross-Team Refinement varies to optimize these two purposes. Where needed, each Scrum Team will continue their own refinement in order for the Product Backlog items to be ready for selection in a Nexus Sprint Planning event.

notes.front: What does an adequately refined Product Backlog minimise during Nexus Sprint Planning?
notes.back: The emergence of new dependencies.
notes.explanation: Refinement, across teams and where needed within each team, gets items ready for selection before the planning event.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Cross-Team Refinement”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Where needed, each Scrum Team will continue their own refinement in order for the Product Backlog items to be ready for selection in a Nexus Sprint Planning event. An adequately refined Product Backlog will minimize the emergence of new dependencies during Nexus Sprint Planning.

notes.front: Nexus Sprint Planning produces a Nexus Sprint Goal. With what does it align, and what does it describe?
notes.back: It aligns with the Product Goal and describes the purpose the Nexus will achieve during the Sprint.
notes.explanation: It links the long-term Product Goal to the work of one Sprint across all the teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Nexus Sprint Goal that aligns with the Product Goal and describes the purpose that will be achieved by the Nexus during the Sprint

notes.front: Which result of Nexus Sprint Planning gives each Scrum Team its own objective, and with what must it align?
notes.back: A Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team, aligned with the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: Each team still has a Sprint Goal, as in Scrum; Nexus adds that it aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal

notes.front: Which single result of Nexus Sprint Planning represents the whole Nexus’s work toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and shows cross-team dependencies?
notes.back: A single Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide says it makes cross-team dependencies transparent, alongside representing the work of the Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a single Nexus Sprint Backlog that represents the work of the Nexus toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and makes cross-team dependencies transparent

notes.front: Which result of Nexus Sprint Planning makes transparent the work one Scrum Team will do in support of the Nexus Sprint Goal?
notes.back: That team’s own Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: Every Scrum Team leaves Nexus Sprint Planning with one, in addition to the single Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team, which makes transparent the work they will do in support of the Nexus Sprint Goal

notes.front: How much detail should a Nexus Sprint Backlog have?
notes.back: Enough that the Nexus can inspect its progress in the Nexus Daily Scrum.
notes.explanation: It is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned. It should have enough detail that the Nexus can inspect their progress in the Nexus Daily Scrum.

notes.front: The commitment for the Nexus Sprint Backlog is the {{c1::Nexus Sprint Goal}}.
notes.explanation: Each Nexus artifact carries a commitment, and this one is a single objective for the Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The commitment for the Nexus Sprint Backlog is the Nexus Sprint Goal. The Nexus Sprint Goal is a single objective for the Nexus.

notes.front: What should the Nexus demonstrate at the Nexus Sprint Review, and to what end?
notes.back: The valuable and useful functionality that is done to achieve the Nexus Sprint Goal, to receive stakeholder feedback.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Teams keep the Nexus Sprint Goal in mind as they work during the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: As Scrum Teams work during the Sprint, they keep the Nexus Sprint Goal in mind. The Nexus should demonstrate the valuable and useful functionality that is done to achieve the Nexus Sprint Goal at the Nexus Sprint Review in order to receive stakeholder feedback.

notes.front: Is the Nexus Daily Scrum the only time Scrum Teams in a Nexus may adjust their plan?
notes.back: No. Cross-team communication can happen throughout the day, to adapt or re-plan the rest of the Sprint’s work.
notes.explanation: The Guide allows more detailed discussions between teams at any time of day.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus Daily Scrum is not the only time Scrum Teams in the Nexus are allowed to adjust their plan. Cross-team communication can occur throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint’s work.

notes.front: How does each Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum complement the Nexus Daily Scrum?
notes.back: By creating plans for the day, focused primarily on the integration issues raised at the Nexus Daily Scrum.
notes.explanation: The team Daily Scrum still takes place; it turns what the Nexus Daily Scrum raised into each team’s plan.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Each Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum complements the Nexus Daily Scrum by creating plans for the day, focused primarily on addressing the integration issues raised during the Nexus Daily Scrum.

notes.front: At the Nexus Sprint Review, must all completed work be shown in detail?
notes.back: No. It may not be possible; the Nexus presents its results and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.
notes.explanation: Attendees then collaborate on what the Nexus should do to address the feedback.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: During the event, the Nexus presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed, although it may not be possible to show all completed work in detail. Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what the Nexus should do to address the feedback.

notes.front: How do the Scrum Teams’ own Sprint Retrospectives relate to the Nexus Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: They complement it, using bottom-up intelligence to focus on issues that affect the Nexus as a whole.
notes.explanation: They do so in addition to individual team improvements, and the Nexus Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: In addition to individual team improvements, the Scrum Teams’ Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective by using bottom-up intelligence to focus on issues that affect the Nexus as a whole. The Nexus Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

notes.front: At scale, at what level must the Product Backlog be understood?
notes.back: At a level where dependencies can be detected and minimised.
notes.explanation: There is one Product Backlog listing what is needed to improve the product for the entire Nexus and all its Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Product Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: There is a single Product Backlog that contains a list of what is needed to improve the product for the entire Nexus and all of its Scrum Teams. At scale, the Product Backlog must be understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimized.

notes.front: In a Nexus, the Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, including its content, {{c1::availability}} and ordering.
notes.explanation: At scale, the same Product Backlog must also be understood well enough to detect and minimise dependencies.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Product Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: At scale, the Product Backlog must be understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimized. The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, including its content, availability, and ordering.

notes.front: In a Nexus, the Increment is done only when {{c1::integrated}}, valuable and usable.
notes.explanation: The Definition of Done defines the state of the integrated work when it meets the quality and measures required for the product.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The commitment for the Integrated Increment is the Definition of Done, which defines the state of the integrated work when it meets the quality and measures required for the product. The Increment is done only when integrated, valuable, and usable.

notes.front: May a Scrum Team in a Nexus use a Definition of Done that differs from the one agreed for the Integrated Increment?
notes.back: Only a more stringent one; it cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed.
notes.explanation: Individual Scrum Teams self-manage to achieve the agreed state, and may go beyond it within their own teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: manage to achieve this state. They may choose to apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.

notes.front: What does the Nexus Guide say about decisions based on artifacts, and why does scale matter?
notes.back: They are only as effective as artifact transparency, and the impact of flawed decisions can be magnified at the scale of Nexus.
notes.explanation: The Guide says incomplete or partial information will lead to incorrect or flawed decisions.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Decisions made based on the state of artifacts are only as effective as the level of artifact transparency. Incomplete or partial information will lead to incorrect or flawed decisions. The impact of those decisions can be magnified at the scale of Nexus.

notes.front: Can an organisation implement only some parts of Nexus and still call it Nexus?
notes.back: No. Implementing only parts is possible, but the result is not Nexus.
notes.explanation: As with Scrum, the accountabilities, artifacts, events and rules of Nexus are immutable.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “End Note”, p. 10
notes.evidence: As with the Scrum framework, the accountabilities in Nexus, its artifacts, events, and rules are immutable. Although implementing only parts of Nexus is possible, the result is not Nexus.

notes.front: A product now has five Scrum Teams. A director proposes adding a weekly status report, an architecture board sign-off for every item and a “feature owner” on each team. The Product Owner is asked how this fits Nexus. What is the best response?
notes.back: A: Nexus extends Scrum only where absolutely necessary to manage dependencies between teams.
notes.choices:
A) Test each proposal against one question: is it absolutely necessary to minimise and manage dependencies between the teams?
B) Accept all three, because Nexus exists to add the coordination that Scrum lacks.
C) Accept them for the first three Sprints, then review whether they helped.
D) Drop the Nexus events to make room for the new meetings.
notes.choicesExplained: B reverses the Guide: Nexus extends Scrum minimally, not wherever coordination could be added. C still adopts them without asking whether each is necessary. D swaps the Nexus framework’s own events for unrelated meetings.
notes.explanation: Nexus builds on Scrum, extending it only where absolutely necessary to minimise and manage dependencies between multiple Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Nexus is a framework for developing and sustaining scaled product delivery initiatives. It builds upon Scrum, extending it only where absolutely necessary to minimize and manage dependencies between multiple Scrum Teams while promoting empiricism and the Scrum Values.

notes.front: Three months into a Nexus, a manager argues that “at this size, Scrum’s rules have to bend”: each team should get its own Product Owner and its own backlog. What should the Product Owner answer?
notes.back: B: scaled Scrum is still Scrum; Nexus does not change its core design or negate its rules.
notes.choices:
A) Agree, because scaled Scrum may adapt Scrum’s rules to fit its size.
B) Disagree: scaled Scrum is still Scrum, and Nexus does not negate Scrum’s rules.
C) Agree, as long as a chief Product Owner settles conflicts between them.
D) Agree for now, and merge the backlogs again before the next release.
notes.choicesExplained: A is the opposite of the Guide, which says Nexus does not negate the rules of Scrum. D still splits one product across several backlogs. C builds a hierarchy of Product Owners, but a Nexus has a single Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide warns that changing Scrum’s core design or negating its rules covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Scaled Scrum is still Scrum. Nexus does not change the core design or ideas of Scrum, or leave out elements, or negate the rules of Scrum. Doing so covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless.

notes.front: Leadership judges a new Nexus by how busy every Developer is. The Product Owner wants a lens that matches the goal of Nexus. Which lens fits?
notes.back: B: Nexus aims to scale the value delivered by reducing the complexity the teams encounter.
notes.choices:
A) Whether every team is fully loaded every Sprint.
B) Whether the teams deliver more value on the single product as the complexity between them falls.
C) Whether more teams can be added each quarter.
D) Whether each team produces as much output as the others.
notes.choicesExplained: A measures activity, not value. C assumes more people means more value, which the Guide says is not always so. D compares team output instead of the value of the integrated product.
notes.explanation: The goal of Nexus is to scale the value that teams on a single product deliver, by reducing the complexity they encounter as they collaborate.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The goal of Nexus is to scale the value that a group of Scrum Teams, working on a single product, is able to deliver. It does this by reducing the complexity that those teams encounter as they collaborate to deliver an integrated, valuable, useful product Increment at least once every Sprint.

notes.front: Two teams in a Nexus keep blocking each other because the pricing rules and the checkout screens live in one tightly coupled module, so almost every change needs both teams. What should the Product Owner encourage the teams to look at?
notes.back: D: change the product structure so the concerns are more independently separated.
notes.choices:
A) Merging the two teams’ Sprint Backlogs into one list.
B) Having one team wait each Sprint while the other finishes.
C) Adding a third team to own the module.
D) The product structure: separating those concerns so each can change independently.
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the dependency in place, and each team still needs its own Sprint Backlog. B works around the dependency instead of reducing it. C adds people, which adds complexity and dependencies.
notes.explanation: How independently concerns are separated in the product greatly affects the complexity of creating an integrated product release.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Product structure: The degree to which different concerns are independently separated in the product will greatly affect the complexity of creating an integrated product release.

notes.front: Teams in a Nexus can only put questions to other teams through a manager, who collects them for a weekly meeting. Items often wait days for an answer. What should the Product Owner raise at the Nexus Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: A: change the communication structure; delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.
notes.choices:
A) Changing the communication structure so teams can talk to each other directly.
B) Padding every forecast to allow for waiting time.
C) Longer Sprints, so answers arrive in time.
D) Holding the manager’s meeting twice a week instead of once.
notes.choicesExplained: C hides the delay inside a longer Sprint instead of removing it. B plans around the delay rather than fixing it. D keeps the same indirect path and only shortens the wait a little.
notes.explanation: The way people communicate within and between teams affects their ability to get work done, and delays in communication and feedback reduce flow.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Communication structure: The way that people communicate within and between teams affects their ability to get work done; delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.

notes.front: A product with seven Scrum Teams is delivering less each quarter, and integration problems take up much of every Sprint. A sponsor offers funding for two more teams. What should the Product Owner consider first?
notes.back: B: scaling down can be an important practice in delivering more value.
notes.choices:
A) Accepting both teams, since more teams means more capacity.
B) Whether fewer people on the product could deliver more value.
C) Accepting one team as a compromise.
D) Giving the new teams a separate backlog so they do not interfere.
notes.choicesExplained: A assumes more people means more value; the Guide says scaling value does not always require that. C still adds people without asking whether it helps. D breaks the single Product Backlog that all teams in a Nexus use.
notes.explanation: More people and a larger product increase complexity, dependencies, the need for collaboration and communication pathways.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions. Scaling-down, reducing the number of people who work on something, can be an important practice in delivering more value.

notes.front: Stakeholders planning a new product assume that “a launch this important needs five teams from day one”. Which argument from the Nexus Guide should the Product Owner bring?
notes.back: D: scaling the value delivered does not always require adding more people.
notes.choices:
A) A Nexus must always start with at least five teams.
B) Five teams will always reach the market faster than one.
C) Scaling is allowed only after the first release.
D) More people bring more complexity, dependencies and communication pathways, so scaling value does not always mean adding people.
notes.choicesExplained: A invents a rule; the Guide describes a Nexus as approximately three to nine teams and never requires five. B assumes more people always means faster delivery, which the Guide contradicts. C invents a timing rule the Guide does not contain.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls this often counterintuitive: adding people and growing the product increases complexity and dependencies.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: While often counterintuitive, scaling the value that is delivered does not always require adding more people. Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions.

notes.front: Near the end of a Sprint, each of four teams reports its own work as done, but nobody has combined the pieces and they have never run together. The Product Owner asks who is accountable for a done Integrated Increment. What is the answer?
notes.back: B: the Nexus Integration Team is accountable for a done Integrated Increment at least once a Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) Each Scrum Team separately, for its own part.
B) The Nexus Integration Team.
C) The Product Owner alone.
D) The stakeholders, at the Nexus Sprint Review.
notes.choicesExplained: A counts separate parts, but the Integrated Increment is the combined work of the Nexus. C: the Product Owner belongs to the Nexus Integration Team, but the accountability is that team’s. D: stakeholders give feedback; they are not accountable for the Increment.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Nexus Integration Team accountable for ensuring the combined work of the Nexus is done at least once a Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring that a done Integrated Increment (the combined work completed by a Nexus) is produced at least once a Sprint.

notes.front: An integration issue appears between two teams’ work. One team says, “That is the Nexus Integration Team’s job now; we will wait for them.” What should the Product Owner, who also sits on the Nexus Integration Team, say?
notes.back: B: Scrum Teams address integration issues; the Nexus Integration Team is the focal point.
notes.choices:
A) Agreed; the Nexus Integration Team does all integration work.
B) The Scrum Teams address integration issues; the Nexus Integration Team is the focal point and draws on their knowledge.
C) The Product Owner will decide the technical fix.
D) Leave it for the Nexus Sprint Retrospective.
notes.choicesExplained: A puts all integration on the Nexus Integration Team, but the Guide says the Scrum Teams address integration issues. C: how work becomes an Increment is for the Developers. D leaves an issue open that threatens a constantly Integrated Increment.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point and should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While Scrum Teams address integration issues within the Nexus, the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration for the Nexus. Integration includes addressing technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a Nexus’ ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment. It should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.

notes.front: The teams cannot integrate because a purchasing rule stops them getting a shared test environment. A Developer says, “That is not technical, so it is not an integration issue.” How should the Product Owner see it?
notes.back: C: integration includes non-technical cross-functional team constraints.
notes.choices:
A) As outside the Nexus, to be left to the purchasing department.
B) As a matter for each team to solve alone.
C) As an integration issue: integration covers non-technical constraints that impede a constantly Integrated Increment.
D) As a reason to relax the Definition of Done until it is fixed.
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores a constraint that is impeding the Nexus. B: the Nexus Integration Team is the focal point for cross-team constraints like this. D: no team may apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.
notes.explanation: The Guide says integration includes technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a constantly Integrated Increment.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While Scrum Teams address integration issues within the Nexus, the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration for the Nexus. Integration includes addressing technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a Nexus’ ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment. It should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.

notes.front: The search team in a Nexus has built a feature that works well alone but breaks other teams’ work when combined. Its members say, “We delivered our part.” Which statement reflects the Product Owner’s accountability?
notes.back: B: the accountability covers the work performed and integrated by the Scrum Teams in the Nexus.
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner is accountable only for ordering; value is the teams’ concern.
B) The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the work performed and integrated by all the teams.
C) The Product Owner should accept the feature, since it passed the team’s own tests.
D) The Product Owner is accountable for each team’s output separately.
notes.choicesExplained: A shrinks the accountability; the Product Owner is accountable for maximising value. D treats the teams’ work separately, but the Guide names the integrated work. C accepts work that does not integrate.
notes.explanation: In a Nexus, the Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product and the work performed and integrated by the Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, and as described in Scrum, a Product Backlog has a single Product Owner who has the final say on its contents. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product and the work performed and integrated by the Scrum Teams in a Nexus.

notes.front: A Nexus has grown to six teams, and the Product Owner cannot attend every team’s refinement. Which approach is consistent with the Nexus Guide?
notes.back: B: how it is done may vary, but the Product Owner stays accountable.
notes.choices:
A) Appoint a Product Owner for each team, each with the final say on their team’s items.
B) Choose ways of working that suit this Nexus while staying accountable for effective Product Backlog management.
C) Let each team keep and order its own copy of the backlog.
D) Hand the backlog accountability to the Nexus Integration Team’s Scrum Master.
notes.choicesExplained: A breaks the single Product Owner who has the final say on the Product Backlog. C breaks the single Product Backlog. D moves an accountability the Guide gives to the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide says how effective Product Backlog management is done may vary widely across organisations, Nexuses, teams and individuals.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management. How this is done may vary widely across organizations, Nexuses, Scrum Teams, and individuals.

notes.front: A senior Developer belongs to the Nexus Integration Team and to the payments team. Mid-Sprint, an issue blocks three teams from integrating, while the payments team needs her on a payments item. What should happen?
notes.back: D: Nexus Integration Team membership takes precedence.
notes.choices:
A) The payments item comes first, because team membership is primary.
B) The issue waits for the next Nexus Sprint Planning.
C) The Product Owner splits her time evenly between the two.
D) The integration issue comes first; she returns to payments work once her Nexus Integration Team responsibility is met.
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the Guide’s precedence. C is not the Product Owner’s call, and the Guide gives the Nexus Integration Team work priority. B leaves three teams blocked for the rest of the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide says this preference helps ensure that work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Membership in the Nexus Integration Team takes precedence over individual Scrum Team membership. As long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as team members of their respective Scrum Teams. This preference helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.

notes.front: The Product Owner hears that members of the Nexus Integration Team “are not allowed to do any Scrum Team work”. What is accurate?
notes.back: B: they may work in their Scrum Teams once their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied.
notes.choices:
A) Correct; they must leave their Scrum Teams.
B) Incorrect; they can work in their Scrum Teams as long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied.
C) Incorrect; Scrum Team work always comes first for them.
D) Correct, but only during Nexus Sprint Planning.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D invent a ban the Guide does not contain; it lets members work in their Scrum Teams. C reverses the precedence the Guide gives to Nexus Integration Team membership.
notes.explanation: Nexus Integration Team membership takes precedence, but members can work as members of their own Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Membership in the Nexus Integration Team takes precedence over individual Scrum Team membership. As long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as team members of their respective Scrum Teams. This preference helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.

notes.front: Before Nexus Sprint Planning, the Product Owner notices that nobody knows which team is likely to take the top items, and two of them quietly depend on an unfinished shared service. What is Cross-Team Refinement for here?
notes.back: C: forecast which team delivers which items, and identify cross-team dependencies.
notes.choices:
A) Letting the Product Owner assign items to teams and hold each team to them.
B) Estimating the whole Product Backlog in detail.
C) Helping the teams forecast which team will deliver which items, and identifying dependencies across teams.
D) Replacing Nexus Sprint Planning for this Sprint.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the teams forecast; the Guide does not have the Product Owner assign work. B: the Guide names forecasting and dependencies, not detailed estimates of everything. D: refinement gets items ready for Nexus Sprint Planning; it does not replace it.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives Cross-Team Refinement at scale these two purposes.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Cross-Team Refinement”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Cross-Team Refinement of the Product Backlog at scale serves a dual purpose: • It helps the Scrum Teams forecast which team will deliver which Product Backlog items. • It identifies dependencies across those teams.

notes.front: For Nexus Sprint Planning, the Product Owner invites every Developer from all eight teams “so nobody misses anything”. The room is chaotic and little is decided. What does the Guide say about who meets?
notes.back: C: appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team, with the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) Only the Product Owner and the Scrum Masters plan.
B) Only the Nexus Integration Team plans, and tells the teams their work afterwards.
C) Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team meet with the Product Owner.
D) Every member of the Nexus must attend every Nexus event.
notes.choicesExplained: B cuts the teams out of their own planning. A leaves out the teams’ representatives, whom the Guide names. D: the Guide says Nexus events are attended by whoever is needed, since full attendance may not be practical at scale.
notes.explanation: The purpose is to coordinate the activities of all Scrum Teams for the Sprint, which representatives and the Product Owner do together.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The purpose of Nexus Sprint Planning is to coordinate the activities of all Scrum Teams within a Nexus for a single Sprint. Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team and the Product Owner meet to plan the Sprint.

notes.front: At the end of Nexus Sprint Planning, the Nexus has a Nexus Sprint Goal and every team has its Sprint Backlog. What is still missing from the results the Guide lists?
notes.back: D: each team’s Sprint Goal and the single Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) A release date for each item.
B) A detailed task plan for the Nexus Integration Team.
C) A risk register for the Sprint.
D) A Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team and a single Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are not among the Guide’s results of Nexus Sprint Planning; its four results are the Nexus Sprint Goal, team Sprint Goals, one Nexus Sprint Backlog and team Sprint Backlogs.
notes.explanation: The single Nexus Sprint Backlog makes cross-team dependencies transparent, and each team’s Sprint Goal aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal ● a single Nexus Sprint Backlog that represents the work of the Nexus toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and makes cross-team dependencies transparent

notes.front: At the Nexus Daily Scrum, representatives take turns listing everything each Developer did yesterday, and it runs long. The Product Owner is attending. How should it be refocused?
notes.back: D: its purpose is integration issues and progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) It should be cancelled, since each team has its own Daily Scrum.
B) On each team’s speed compared with the others.
C) On refining next Sprint’s items.
D) On integration issues, newly found cross-team dependencies and progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.choicesExplained: B compares teams instead of inspecting the integrated Increment. C turns it into refinement, which is a different activity. A removes the event the team Daily Scrums complement.
notes.explanation: The representatives inspect the current state of the integrated Increment and identify integration issues and new cross-team dependencies.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Nexus Daily Scrum is to identify any integration issues and inspect progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal. Appropriate representatives from the Scrum Teams attend the Nexus Daily Scrum, inspect the current state of the integrated Increment, and identify integration issues and newly discovered cross-team dependencies or impacts.

notes.front: Stakeholders ask for four separate demos at the Nexus Sprint Review, one per team, each covering everything that team touched. What should the Product Owner propose?
notes.back: D: the review covers the Integrated Increment; not all work need be shown in detail.
notes.choices:
A) Four separate team Sprint Reviews instead of one Nexus event.
B) A written list of every item, with no demonstration.
C) Postponing the review until every item can be shown.
D) One review of the done Integrated Increment and progress toward the Product Goal, even if not all work is shown in detail.
notes.choicesExplained: A brings back team Sprint Reviews, which the Nexus Sprint Review replaces. B drops the presentation of results. C delays feedback; the Guide expects that not all work may be shown in detail.
notes.explanation: The Guide accepts that not all completed work may be shown in detail, and attendees collaborate on how to address the feedback.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: During the event, the Nexus presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed, although it may not be possible to show all completed work in detail. Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what the Nexus should do to address the feedback.

notes.front: A Scrum Team in a Nexus wants to keep holding its own Sprint Review “for our own stakeholders”, as well as the Nexus Sprint Review. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: B: the Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.
notes.choices:
A) That is fine; team Sprint Reviews run alongside the Nexus Sprint Review.
B) The Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual team Sprint Reviews, so those stakeholders should come to it.
C) Only if those stakeholders cannot attend the Nexus Sprint Review.
D) Only in Sprints with no integration issues.
notes.choicesExplained: A contradicts the Guide, which replaces team Sprint Reviews. C and D invent exceptions the Guide does not contain.
notes.explanation: The entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, which is why one review replaces the team reviews.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Since the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, a Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.

notes.front: A Scrum Master in a Nexus proposes dropping the team Sprint Retrospectives “just as we dropped the team Sprint Reviews”. Which reply is right?
notes.back: A: team Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective.
notes.choices:
A) Only the team Sprint Reviews are replaced; team Sprint Retrospectives still happen and complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective.
B) Agree; Nexus replaces every team event with a Nexus event.
C) Agree, but only in Sprints with few integration issues.
D) Agree, if the Nexus Sprint Retrospective runs twice as long.
notes.choicesExplained: B overstates the rule; the Guide replaces only the Sprint Review. C and D invent conditions for dropping an event the Guide keeps.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the teams’ own Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective, using bottom-up intelligence on issues that affect the whole Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: In addition to individual team improvements, the Scrum Teams’ Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective by using bottom-up intelligence to focus on issues that affect the Nexus as a whole. The Nexus Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

notes.front: Four teams each propose a Sprint Goal for their own area: faster search, a new logo, a billing report and an admin screen. None of them connect. What should the Product Owner push for at Nexus Sprint Planning?
notes.back: D: one Nexus Sprint Goal that creates coherence and focus across the teams.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the four goals as they are; each team’s own focus is enough.
B) Pick the most valuable team goal and let the other teams work without one.
C) Let each team’s stakeholders decide its goal.
D) A Nexus Sprint Goal that brings the teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves four separate initiatives with no coherence. B leaves teams without Sprint Goals, which every Scrum Team has. C hands the goal to stakeholders instead of the Nexus.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Sprint Goal creates coherence and focus by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Goal is a single objective for the Nexus. It is the sum of all the work and Sprint Goals of the Scrum Teams within the Nexus. It creates coherence and focus for the Nexus for the Sprint by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

notes.front: The Nexus Sprint Goal is “First paying customers in the new region”. One team proposes a Sprint Goal about an internal report that does nothing toward it. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: A: each team’s Sprint Goal aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) Each team’s Sprint Goal should align with the Nexus Sprint Goal, so rework it to support that goal.
B) That is fine; team Sprint Goals are independent of the Nexus Sprint Goal.
C) Replace the Nexus Sprint Goal with the report.
D) Let the team work without a Sprint Goal this Sprint.
notes.choicesExplained: B contradicts the Guide, which makes team Sprint Goals align with the Nexus Sprint Goal. C lets one team override the whole Nexus’s objective. D leaves a Scrum Team without a Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: Nexus Sprint Planning produces a Sprint Goal for each team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal

notes.front: The Product Backlog for a Nexus holds large items such as “Improve onboarding”, and every Nexus Sprint Planning uncovers surprise cross-team dependencies. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: D: at scale, the Product Backlog must be understood well enough to detect and minimise dependencies.
notes.choices:
A) Keep items large so that teams have freedom.
B) Let each team keep a private list of its own dependencies.
C) Give every item with a dependency to one team permanently.
D) Work with the teams so items are understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimised.
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the dependencies hidden until planning. B hides them from the other teams instead of making them transparent. C ignores what the dependency is and overloads one team.
notes.explanation: At scale, the single Product Backlog must be understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimised.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Product Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: There is a single Product Backlog that contains a list of what is needed to improve the product for the entire Nexus and all of its Scrum Teams. At scale, the Product Backlog must be understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimized.

notes.front: A team in the Nexus wants to reorder the top of the Product Backlog so its own items come first, arguing that it “knows the dependencies best”. How should the Product Owner respond?
notes.back: B: the Product Owner stays accountable for content, availability and ordering, informed by the teams.
notes.choices:
A) Allow it, since ordering is the teams’ decision in a Nexus.
B) Use the team’s dependency knowledge but keep the ordering decision, since the Product Owner is accountable for it.
C) Hand ordering to the Nexus Integration Team.
D) Create a separate backlog for that team.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C move ordering away from the Product Owner, who is accountable for it. D breaks the single Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog’s content, availability and ordering, and dependencies must be detected and minimised.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Product Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: At scale, the Product Backlog must be understood at a level where dependencies can be detected and minimized. The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, including its content, availability, and ordering.

notes.front: Midway through a Sprint, the Nexus has a done Integrated Increment with a feature a key customer is waiting for. A stakeholder asks whether they must wait for the Nexus Sprint Review. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: A: the Integrated Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) No; it is inspected at the Nexus Sprint Review, but may be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.
B) Yes; nothing may be delivered before the Nexus Sprint Review.
C) Yes, unless every team agrees in a vote.
D) No, and the Nexus Sprint Review can then be skipped.
notes.choicesExplained: B contradicts the Guide, which allows delivery before the end of the Sprint. C invents a vote. D: the Integrated Increment is still inspected at the Nexus Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: Delivering early is allowed, provided the Integrated Increment meets the Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Integrated Increment”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Integrated Increment is inspected at the Nexus Sprint Review, but may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint. The Integrated Increment must meet the Definition of Done.

notes.front: Three teams each finished their part of a feature and met the Definition of Done in their own environments, but the parts have not been combined. A stakeholder asks whether the feature is done. What is accurate?
notes.back: B: in a Nexus, the Increment is done only when integrated, valuable and usable.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; each part met the Definition of Done.
B) No; the Increment is done only when integrated, valuable and usable.
C) Partly; count it as done now and integrate it next Sprint.
D) Yes, if two of the three parts are integrated.
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores integration, which the Guide requires. D accepts partial integration. C counts unintegrated work as done.
notes.explanation: The Definition of Done defines the state of the integrated work when it meets the quality and measures required for the product.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The commitment for the Integrated Increment is the Definition of Done, which defines the state of the integrated work when it meets the quality and measures required for the product. The Increment is done only when integrated, valuable, and usable.

notes.front: Two teams in a new Nexus each want to write their own Definition of Done from scratch, with different rules. Who is responsible for the Definition of Done for the Integrated Increment?
notes.back: A: the Nexus Integration Team; every team must define and adhere to it.
notes.choices:
A) The Nexus Integration Team; all Scrum Teams in the Nexus must define and adhere to it.
B) Each team, for its own part, with no shared definition.
C) The Product Owner alone.
D) The organisation’s quality department.
notes.choicesExplained: B leaves the Integrated Increment with no single Definition of Done. C and D name people the Guide does not make responsible.
notes.explanation: The Definition of Done must be one that can be applied to the Integrated Increment developed each Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for a Definition of Done that can be applied to the Integrated Increment developed each Sprint. All Scrum Teams within the Nexus must define and adhere to this Definition of Done.

notes.front: One team in a Nexus wants to add a load test to its own Definition of Done, beyond what the Nexus agreed. Another asks to skip the agreed security scan “this Sprint only”. What should the Product Owner support?
notes.back: B: teams may be stricter, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed.
notes.choices:
A) Both, since teams self-manage their own Definition of Done.
B) The stricter Definition for the first team, but not the weaker one for the second.
C) Neither, since every team must use exactly the same criteria.
D) The weaker one only, if the Product Owner accepts the risk.
notes.choicesExplained: A allows less rigorous criteria, which the Guide forbids. C forbids a stricter Definition, which the Guide allows. D: accepting risk does not permit less rigorous criteria.
notes.explanation: Teams may apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but never a less rigorous one.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: manage to achieve this state. They may choose to apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.

notes.front: Facing a deadline, a stakeholder asks the Product Owner to let one team relax the agreed Definition of Done so its feature can be shown at the Nexus Sprint Review. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: C: a team cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.
notes.choices:
A) Agree, since the Product Owner decides the Definition of Done.
B) Agree, if the feature is labelled as a trial.
C) Decline; no team may apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.
D) Agree, and plan to fix the quality next Sprint.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Nexus Integration Team, not the Product Owner alone, is responsible for this Definition of Done. B and D still let one team work below the agreed criteria.
notes.explanation: The Guide allows a team a stricter Definition of Done, never a weaker one.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: manage to achieve this state. They may choose to apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.

notes.front: In a Nexus, which team Scrum event does the Nexus Guide say is replaced, and which team events does it say complement Nexus events?
notes.back: Team Sprint Reviews are replaced by the Nexus Sprint Review; team Daily Scrums and Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Daily Scrum and Nexus Sprint Retrospective.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives the reason for the Sprint Review: the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for stakeholder feedback.
notes.contrast: Nexus Daily Scrum and Nexus Sprint Retrospective: added to the team events, which complement them.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Since the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, a Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.

notes.front: Under the Scrum Guide alone, how do several Scrum Teams on one product arrive at their Definition of Done?
notes.back: They must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide leaves it to the teams together; Nexus names who is responsible.
notes.contrast: Nexus Guide: the Nexus Integration Team is responsible for the Definition of Done for the Integrated Increment, and every team must define and adhere to it.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

notes.front: In a Nexus, how does the Product Goal differ from the Nexus Sprint Goal as a commitment?
notes.back: The Product Goal is the Product Backlog’s commitment and the Nexus’s long-term goal; the Nexus Sprint Goal is one Sprint’s objective.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal describes the future state of the product.
notes.contrast: Nexus Sprint Goal: the commitment for the Nexus Sprint Backlog, a single objective for the Nexus in one Sprint, aligned with the Product Goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Product Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The commitment for the Product Backlog is the Product Goal. The Product Goal, which describes the future state of the product and serves as a long-term goal of the Nexus.
